title: Cuisine
description: Hyderabadi cuisine — a kitchen at the crossroads of empires. Biryani, haleem, marag, lukhmi and khubani ka meetha.
dedication: In memory of the Asaf Jahi dynasty
title_html: A kitchen at the crossroads of empires
subtitle: Persian saffron, Telugu chilli, Marathi grain, Mughal patience

sections.title_html: A kitchen at the crossroads of empires
sections.sub: Where the Persian khansamas of the court met the Telugu cooks of the plateau
body: Hyderabadi cuisine was born when the Persian khansamas of the Asaf Jahi court met the Telugu cooks of the deccan plateau. The result was a kitchen that took the long, slow techniques of Mughal high cuisine and married them to the heat of South Indian masalas — a marriage you can still taste in any neighbourhood biryani house.<cite data-ref="collingham-2006 leonard-1978"></cite>

aside.label: A Dakhni table

items.value: Slow-cooked basmati and meat sealed under dough — the signature of Hyderabad.
Wheat, lentils and meat pounded for hours into a Ramazan staple.
A clear mutton broth, traditionally served at dawn.
A square mince-stuffed pastry from the Hyderabadi wedding table.
Long green chillies in a peanut-tamarind gravy.
Lightly spiced rice with whole cumin — the everyday partner to a curry.
Stewed apricots topped with thick cream — the close of any feast.
Strong, milky tea drawn slowly — the rhythm of the old city.

aside.note: A Dakhni feast is judged by the kachchi biryani — meat marinated raw, layered with rice and cooked in one sealed pot. Anything else is pakki, and Hyderabad will tell you the difference.

sections.sub: Meat marinated raw, layered with rice, sealed and slow-cooked
body: The signature dish is kachchi dum biryani: meat marinated raw in yoghurt, ginger, fried onions and spice, layered with rice that has been parboiled separately, sealed under a dough lid and cooked over slow embers until the steam alone has done the work. Nothing about it is hurried. Done well, the meat is melting, the rice is dry-grained, and every spoonful carries saffron at one bite and chilli at the next.

sections.sub: Haleem, marag, mirchi ka salan and the everyday Hyderabadi table
body: Around the biryani sits a wider table: haleem in the month of Ramazan, marag for early-morning weddings, mirchi ka salan and bagara khana for any ordinary lunch, lukhmi for the high days, and khubani ka meetha — stewed Saksaul apricots under a slick of cream — to send the guests home. A glass of Irani chai ties it all together.<cite data-ref="leonard-1978"></cite>

items.text: With the founding of Hyderabad by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah, the new city's court kitchen draws together Persian, Mughal, and Deccani culinary traditions for the first time.<cite data-ref="britannica-biryani"></cite>

The Asaf Jahi court establishes Hyderabad as its capital; Persian khansamas arrive carrying the slow techniques of Mughal high cuisine — dum cooking, saffron, dried fruits — into the Telugu kitchen of the plateau.<cite data-ref="leonard-1978 collingham-2006"></cite>

Kachchi dum biryani is codified at the Asaf Jahi court: meat marinated raw in yoghurt and spice, layered with parboiled rice, sealed under a dough lid, and cooked over slow embers.<cite data-ref="britannica-biryani"></cite>
Haleem — wheat, lentils, and meat pounded for hours — becomes Hyderabad's communal Ramazan staple, prepared in neighbourhood kitchens across the city.
Marag, lukhmi, mirchi ka salan, and bagara khana find their fixed places in the Hyderabadi feast order, from pre-dawn wedding broth to the everyday lunch table.<cite data-ref="leonard-1978"></cite>
Khubani ka meetha — stewed Saksaul apricots under a slick of thick cream — is established as the conventional close of a Hyderabadi feast.

Irani café culture arrives through Persian commercial connections; Irani chai — strong, milky tea drawn slowly — becomes the defining rhythm of the old city's public life.<cite data-ref="leonard-1978"></cite>

The kachchi versus pakki biryani distinction survives as a point of local knowledge and civic pride; the Hyderabadi table continues to fuse court Persian technique with the heat of the Deccani masala.

references.text: Lizzie Collingham, Curry: A Tale of Cooks and Conquerors, Oxford University Press, 2006.
Karen Leonard, Social History of an Indian Caste: The Kayasths of Hyderabad, University of California Press, 1978.
